units.title: Unit 43 — Negative opinions about people
learningObjectives: Recognise idiomatic expressions of blame, contempt and disapproval and identify their strength and register.
Contrast direct criticism with more measured professional evaluations of behaviour.
Use combinations for responsibility, judgement, trust and dissatisfaction in natural contexts.

items.example: The supervisor accused the team of being bone idle, although they had worked all weekend.
items.note: Bone idle is an informal and strongly disapproving way to describe extreme laziness.

items.pt: ter uma atitude difícil ou pouco cooperativa
items.example: The coach said that a talented player can still have an attitude problem.
items.note: An attitude problem suggests a persistently negative or uncooperative manner.

items.example: The agent seemed like a slippery customer who never gave the same answer twice.
items.note: Slippery customer is informal and implies that someone is evasive or difficult to trust.

items.example: Local residents condemned the mindless violence that followed the match.
items.note: Mindless suggests violence without thought, purpose or consideration for its consequences.

items.example: Instead of discussing the decision, he tried to pick a fight with the organiser.
items.note: Pick a fight means deliberately start a quarrel or provoke a confrontation.

items.example: The principal claimed that a few pupils had no respect for authority.
items.note: Have no respect for conveys a negative judgement about attitudes towards those in charge.

items.example: Some senior staff appeared to hold the new manager in contempt.
items.note: Hold someone in contempt is a formal, severe expression of disdain.

items.pt: levar a culpa ou receber críticas
items.example: The spokesperson had to take the flak for a policy she had not designed.
items.note: Take the flak means receive harsh criticism or blame, often on behalf of others.

items.example: The coordinator described the constant interruptions as a disruptive influence on the group.
items.note: A disruptive influence is a person or factor that makes normal activity harder.

items.example: Repeated personal accusations began to poison the atmosphere in the office.
items.note: Poison the atmosphere is figurative: it means make a social setting unpleasant or hostile.

items.pt: a responsabilidade pela culpa recai sobre
items.example: The report concluded that the blame rests with those who approved the unsafe procedure.
items.note: The blame rests with assigns responsibility for an undesirable outcome.

items.pt: diretamente e sem margem para dúvidas
items.example: Responsibility for the mistake lies fairly and squarely with the management team.
items.note: Fairly and squarely reinforces that blame or responsibility is clear and unambiguous.

items.example: A director cannot shirk responsibilities when a critical safety issue is reported.
items.note: Shirk responsibilities means deliberately avoid duties that should be fulfilled.

items.example: I was disappointed that an experienced journalist would stoop to that level.
items.note: Stoop to that level criticises conduct considered beneath someone’s standards.

items.example: The rival company tried to play a dirty trick by circulating a false rumour.
items.note: A dirty trick is a dishonest or unfair action designed to harm or mislead.

items.pt: uma pessoa muito desagradável e mal-intencionada
items.example: People avoided the contractor because he had a reputation as a nasty piece of work.
items.note: A nasty piece of work is an informal, forcefully negative description of a person.

items.example: Insulting a colleague in front of clients was totally out of order.
items.note: In British English, out of order can condemn unacceptable behaviour, not only a broken machine.

items.example: The way the residents were treated was a downright disgrace.
items.note: Downright strongly intensifies disgrace and expresses indignation.

items.pt: não confiar nem um pouco em alguém
items.example: After three conflicting explanations, I would not trust that salesman an inch.
items.note: Not trust someone an inch is a forceful informal way to express complete distrust.

items.example: The committee described the threats as utterly unacceptable behaviour.
items.note: Utterly intensifies unacceptable; this is a useful formal alternative to angry exclamations.

items.example: The supervisor appeared to show contempt for the concerns raised by junior staff.
items.note: Show contempt for expresses open disrespect, unlike the more internal hold in contempt.

items.example: The adviser betrayed her clients’ trust by sharing confidential details.
items.note: Betray someone’s trust means violate confidence that another person placed in you.

items.example: The reviewer criticised the findings without trying to belittle the researchers’ achievements.
items.note: Belittle achievements means make genuine successes seem less important than they are.

items.example: Personal loyalty can cloud a manager’s judgement during a disciplinary hearing.
items.note: Cloud judgement means negatively affect clear or impartial decision-making.

items.example: I had a few minor niggles about the layout, but the overall design worked well.
items.note: Niggles are small complaints or annoyances, often less serious than a major objection.

items.example: The final chart contained a glaring error that escaped the initial review.
items.note: Glaring combines with error to describe a mistake that should be easy to notice.

items.example: Their constant nagging about the timetable made the atmosphere increasingly tense.
items.note: Nagging refers to repeated complaining or criticism that becomes irritating.

items.example: Residents expressed deep dissatisfaction with the handling of the complaint.
items.note: Deep dissatisfaction is idiomatic; strong dissatisfaction is less conventional in this context.

items.example: Even an experienced editor may overlook a mistake in a lengthy document.
items.note: Overlook a mistake means fail to notice it, not deliberately forgive it.

items.example: The department head agreed to take responsibility for the faulty decision.
items.note: Take responsibility for is a neutral alternative to the more accusatory blame rests with.

items.example: Publishing the private message was a serious lapse in judgement.
items.note: A lapse in judgement denotes a bad decision rather than a permanent lack of ability.

items.example: The proposal drew harsh criticism from residents and local organisations.
items.note: Draw criticism is a conventional way to say that an action attracts negative reactions.

items.example: The mentor worried that peer pressure had become a negative influence on the trainees.
items.note: Influence on names the person or group affected; it can be compared with disruptive influence.

units.title: Unit 44 — References
learningObjectives: Use formal academic and professional collocations when describing qualifications and experience.
Distinguish natural adjective–noun and verb–noun combinations in recommendations and references.
Select appropriate expressions of endorsement, competence, confidence and interpersonal ability.

items.pt: atuar como pessoa de referência ou recomendante
items.example: Professor Liao agreed to act as a referee for the scholarship applicant.
items.note: A referee in this context supplies an academic or professional recommendation.

items.example: During the interview, the applicant demonstrated a keen interest in marine conservation.
items.note: Keen combines naturally with interest to express strong enthusiasm.

items.example: She may lack experience in the field, but she is eager to learn.
items.note: Lack is a transitive verb here, so do not add of before experience.

items.word: make up for a lack of experience
items.example: Her detailed preparation helped make up for a lack of experience in public speaking.
items.note: Make up for means compensate for a disadvantage with another strength.

items.example: The archivist has an encyclopaedic knowledge of the region’s history.
items.note: Encyclopaedic emphasises exceptionally broad and detailed knowledge.

items.pt: adquirir experiência prática ao longo do tempo
items.example: Volunteering allowed the trainees to accumulate practical experience before graduation.
items.note: Accumulate collocates with experience gained gradually through repeated activities.

items.example: The internship allowed her to hone practical skills in laboratory analysis.
items.note: Hone means refine an existing ability through focused practice.

items.example: The fellowship gave him time to pursue an interest in medieval manuscripts.
items.note: Pursue an interest means actively develop or continue an area of personal curiosity.

items.example: Protecting participants’ personal information is of paramount importance to the project.
items.note: Paramount is formal and means more important than virtually anything else.

items.example: The panel believed the candidate could meet the challenges of a demanding course.
items.note: Meet challenges means respond adequately to difficult requirements.

items.example: After her first field trip, she developed a keen interest in archaeology.
items.note: Develop an interest describes how enthusiasm arises; keen intensifies its strength.

items.example: Part-time research work helped the student build relevant experience for postgraduate study.
items.note: Build experience is a natural contemporary alternative to accumulate experience.

items.pt: fornecer uma carta ou declaração de recomendação
items.example: The former supervisor offered to provide a reference for the candidate.
items.note: Provide a reference means give an assessment of somebody’s suitability.

items.example: I would wholeheartedly recommend the engineer for a senior design role.
items.note: Wholeheartedly signals strong and sincere support for a recommendation.

items.example: I have every confidence in her ability to coordinate the next phase.
items.note: This formal phrase expresses complete confidence in someone’s capabilities.

items.example: The assessment showed that the trainee could perform tasks accurately under pressure.
items.note: Perform tasks is relatively formal; carry out tasks is a common alternative.

items.example: Her financial acumen helped the nonprofit manage its limited resources.
items.note: Acumen is sharp practical judgement, especially in business or finance.

items.example: A strong mediator needs excellent interpersonal skills as well as technical expertise.
items.note: Interpersonal skills concern communication and relations with other people.

items.pt: uma pessoa que trabalha bem em equipe
items.example: The project lead described the new analyst as a good team player.
items.note: Team player is a person who cooperates effectively with colleagues.

items.example: The placement revealed a remarkable talent for solving complex design problems.
items.note: Reveal a talent means show an ability that was previously unnoticed or unproven.

items.example: I trust the laboratory coordinator implicitly with confidential records.
items.note: Implicitly intensifies trust and expresses complete confidence in the person.

items.word: an invaluable member of the team
items.example: Within months, the trainee became an invaluable member of the team.
items.note: Invaluable means extremely useful or important; it does not mean without value.

items.example: The institute decided to offer the strongest applicant a permanent position.
items.note: Offer a position is conventional formal recruitment language.

items.example: The role involves a wide range of tasks, from scheduling to data analysis.
items.note: Wide range naturally describes varied responsibilities in job descriptions.

items.example: The founders admired her business acumen during the expansion.
items.note: Business acumen focuses on practical commercial judgement.

items.example: The negotiator’s political acumen helped secure support across parties.
items.note: Political acumen is skill in understanding and navigating political situations.

items.example: The committee acknowledged her highly valued contributions to the programme.
items.note: Highly valued signals strong appreciation and is standard in formal endorsements.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The candidate has advanced computer skills and can manage complex databases.
items.note: Advanced modifies computer skills more naturally than high in a reference.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The role requires a highly educated specialist with strong analytical skills.
items.note: Highly educated is preferred to saying that a person has a high education.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: Applicants should have a good level of education and relevant practical experience.
items.note: Level of education is a natural noun phrase; high education alone is unnatural.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: A well-qualified engineer reviewed the structural calculations.
items.note: Well-qualified is a conventional pre-noun adjective for professional credentials.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: She has good qualifications for the role despite limited management experience.
items.note: Good qualifications is more idiomatic here than high qualifications.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The translator demonstrated an advanced knowledge of English during the assessment.
items.note: Advanced knowledge is a natural collocation, unlike high knowledge.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The curator has an extensive knowledge of contemporary sculpture.
items.note: Extensive knowledge emphasises breadth across a field, unlike large knowledge.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: A comprehensive knowledge of the regulations is essential for this position.
items.note: Comprehensive suggests detailed coverage of most important aspects of a subject.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: He brings considerable experience in supervising international research teams.
items.note: Considerable experience is a standard formal collocation rather than big experience.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The consultant worked hard to establish a good relationship with the community.
items.note: Establish a relationship means form a connection where one did not previously exist.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: Regular feedback helped the new director develop a good relationship with staff.
items.note: Develop a relationship suggests building and strengthening a connection over time.

items.word: a highly valued member of staff
items.pt: um integrante muito valorizado da equipe
items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: Before retiring, she had become a highly valued member of staff.
items.note: Highly valued expresses appreciation; very appreciated is not the usual formulation.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: Reliability is a highly prized quality in emergency response teams.
items.note: Highly prized emphasises that a quality or possession is considered especially valuable.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: A highly placed official confirmed that the policy was under review.
items.note: Highly placed describes senior rank or influential status, not affection.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The specialist was qualified to perform an operation without additional supervision.
items.note: Perform an operation is standard in medical contexts; carry out is also possible.

items.section: C · Correct combinations in formal evaluations
items.example: The choir was invited to perform a song at the opening ceremony.
items.note: Perform can also refer to presenting music for an audience.
